claim: Drug resistance remains a major obstacle to malaria control and eradication efforts.
source: Drug resistance remains a major obstacle to malaria control and eradication efforts, necessitating the development of novel therapeutic strategies to treat this disease.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of malaria control that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Drug combinations based on collateral sensitivity have been proposed as an evolutionary strategy to suppress the emergence of resistance in pathogen populations.
source: Drug combinations based on collateral sensitivity, wherein resistance to one drug causes increased sensitivity to the partner drug, have been proposed as an evolutionary strategy to suppress the emergence of resistance in pathogen populations.
evidence: This statement references a proposed strategy in the literature, implying citation-based support.

claim: TCMDC-125334 was active against all DHODH mutant lines tested, including the DHODH C276Y line.
source: We focus on one compound, TCMDC-125334, which was active against all mutant lines tested, including the DHODH C276Y line, which arose in selections with the clinical candidate DSM265.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the study.

claim: In six selections with TCMDC-125334, the most common mechanism of resistance was copy number variation of the dhodh locus.
source: In six selections with TCMDC-125334, the most common mechanism of resistance to this compound was copy number variation of the dhodh locus, although we did identify one mutation, DHODH I263S, which conferred resistance to TCMDC-125334 but not DSM265.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from resistance selections performed in the study.

claim: The DHODH I263S mutation conferred resistance to TCMDC-125334 but not DSM265.
source: In six selections with TCMDC-125334, the most common mechanism of resistance to this compound was copy number variation of the dhodh locus, although we did identify one mutation, DHODH I263S, which conferred resistance to TCMDC-125334 but not DSM265.
evidence: This is supported by experimental dose-response data presented in the study.

claim: Selection of the DHODH C276Y mutant with TCMDC-125334 yielded additional genetic changes in the dhodh locus.
source: We found that selection of the DHODH C276Y mutant with TCMDC-125334 yielded additional genetic changes in the dhodh locus.
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing data from sequential selection experiments.

claim: Double mutant parasites (DHODH C276Y with additional mutations) exhibited decreased sensitivity to TCMDC-125334 and were highly resistant to DSM265.
source: These double mutant parasites exhibited decreased sensitivity to TCMDC-125334 and were highly resistant to DSM265.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response assay data presented in the study.

claim: Simultaneous exposure of wildtype parasites to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 selected for parasites with a DHODH V532A mutation.
source: Finally, we tested whether collateral sensitivity could be exploited to suppress the emergence of resistance in the context of combination treatment by exposing wildtype parasites to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 simultaneously. This selected for parasites with a DHODH V532A mutation which were cross-resistant to both compounds and were as fit as the wildtype parent in vitro.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from combination selection experiments and whole-genome sequencing.

claim: Parasites with the DHODH V532A mutation were cross-resistant to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334.
source: This selected for parasites with a DHODH V532A mutation which were cross-resistant to both compounds and were as fit as the wildtype parent in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by dose-response assay data showing resistance to both compounds.

claim: Parasites with the DHODH V532A mutation were as fit as the wildtype parent in vitro.
source: This selected for parasites with a DHODH V532A mutation which were cross-resistant to both compounds and were as fit as the wildtype parent in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by competitive growth assay data presented in the study.

claim: Antimicrobial resistance is widely recognized as one of the greatest public health threats of the 21st century.
source: Antimicrobial resistance threatens our ability to combat multiple infectious agents, and is widely recognized as one of the greatest public health threats of the 21st century (Jee et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Jee et al., 2018.

claim: The emergence of resistance in Plasmodium parasite populations and subsequent treatment failure has been documented for all antimalarial drugs in clinical use, including frontline artemisinin combination therapies.
source: The emergence of resistance in Plasmodium parasite populations and subsequent treatment failure has been documented for all antimalarial drugs in clinical use, including frontline artemisinin combination therapies (Haldar et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Haldar et al., 2018.

claim: DHODH is an electron transport chain protein that catalyzes the oxidation of dihydroorotate in orotic acid, which is the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine biosynthesis.
source: DHODH is an electron transport chain protein that catalyzes the oxidation of dihydroorotate in orotic acid, which is the rate-limiting step of pyrimidine biosynthesis.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about the DHODH enzyme.

claim: In Plasmodium, the DHODH reaction is dependent on flavin mononucleotide and ubiquinone cofactors and is coupled to mitochondrial respiration.
source: In Plasmodium, this reaction is dependent on flavin mononucleotide and ubiquinone cofactors and is coupled to mitochondrial respiration.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge about Plasmodium DHODH.

claim: Plasmodium lacks pyrimidine scavenging pathways, making DHODH essential for parasite growth and survival.
source: Because Plasmodium lacks pyrimidine scavenging pathways, this enzyme is essential for parasite growth and survival (Phillips and Rathod, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Phillips and Rathod, 2010.

claim: Multiple high-throughput screens have identified DHODH as a drug target in Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Multiple high-throughput screens have identified DHODH as a drug target in Plasmodium falciparum (Baldwin et al., 2005; Pavadai et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2008), and the triazolopyrimidine-based DHODH inhibitor DSM265 was developed as a clinical antimalarial candidate (Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: DSM265 was developed as a clinical antimalarial candidate.
source: Multiple high-throughput screens have identified DHODH as a drug target in Plasmodium falciparum (Baldwin et al., 2005; Pavadai et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2008; Ross et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2008), and the triazolopyrimidine-based DHODH inhibitor DSM265 was developed as a clinical antimalarial candidate (Phillips et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 2015.

claim: DSM265 showed promising activity in pre-clinical and clinical studies.
source: While the clinical DHODH inhibitor candidate DSM265 showed promising activity in pre-clinical and clinical studies (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2018; McCarthy et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2015; Sulyok et al., 2017), we previously demonstrated that resistance to DSM265 emerges rapidly both in vitro and in a humanized mouse model of P. falciparum infection (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Resistance to DSM265 emerges rapidly both in vitro and in a humanized mouse model of P. falciparum infection.
source: While the clinical DHODH inhibitor candidate DSM265 showed promising activity in pre-clinical and clinical studies (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2018; McCarthy et al., 2017; Murphy et al., 2018; Phillips et al., 2015; Sulyok et al., 2017), we previously demonstrated that resistance to DSM265 emerges rapidly both in vitro and in a humanized mouse model of P. falciparum infection (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandt et al., 2019, which is the authors' previous work.

claim: Resistance to DSM265 was primarily conferred by point mutations in the dhodh locus.
source: Resistance was primarily conferred by point mutations in the dhodh locus.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental data from the authors' prior work.

claim: In Phase 2 clinical trials with DSM265, 2 out of 24 patients failed treatment due to resistance, with recrudescent parasites harboring mutations in dhodh including DHODH C276Y, C276F, and G181S.
source: In Phase 2 clinical trials with DSM265, 2 out of 24 patients failed treatment due to resistance, with recrudescent parasites harboring mutations in dhodh including DHODH C276Y, C276F, and G181S (Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Llanos-Cuentas et al., 2018.

claim: The C276Y and C276F mutations were observed in in vitro resistance selections, as was DHODH G181C.
source: The C276Y and C276F mutations were also observed in in vitro resistance selections, as was DHODH G181C (Phillips et al., 2015; Mandt et al., 2019; White et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The point mutations C276F and G181D were observed in an in vivo selection model.
source: The point mutations C276F and G181D were observed in our in vivo selection model (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandt et al., 2019.

claim: A common strategy to counter the evolution of resistance is to utilize a combination of two or more drugs with distinct antimicrobial mechanisms.
source: A common strategy to counter the evolution of resistance is to utilize a combination of two or more drugs with distinct antimicrobial mechanisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge in antimicrobial treatment strategies.

claim: The basic rationale for combination therapy is that the probability that two resistance mutations would occur simultaneously is much lower than the probability of acquiring resistance to each drug separately.
source: The basic rationale for this strategy is that even if there is some probability of an organism acquiring resistance to each drug separately, the probability that two resistance mutations would occur simultaneously is much lower.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on probability theory applied to drug resistance.

claim: Combination therapy is the standard of treatment for malaria, tuberculosis, and HIV/AIDS.
source: Combination therapy is the standard of treatment for malaria (Hastings, 2011), tuberculosis (Kerantzas and Jacobs, 2017), and HIV/AIDS (Cihlar and Fordyce, 2016), and is increasingly being recommended for the treatment of other bacterial infections (Schmid et al., 2019; Coates et al., 2020; Bodie et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Multidrug resistance has emerged in many major human pathogens, complicating patient treatment and threatening public health efforts.
source: However, multidrug resistance has emerged in many major human pathogens, complicating patient treatment and threatening public health efforts to control the spread of disease (Hamilton et al., 2019; Manson et al., 2017; Dheda et al., 2017; Gregson et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Large-scale bacterial evolution studies have shown that certain combinations of inhibitors can actually accelerate the emergence of resistance compared to treatment with a single inhibitor.
source: Large-scale bacterial evolution studies have also shown that certain combinations of inhibitors can actually accelerate the emergence of resistance compared to treatment with a single inhibitor (Hegreness et al., 2008; Dean et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hegreness et al., 2008 and Dean et al., 2020.

claim: Collateral sensitivity is a phenomenon in which resistance to one drug causes increased sensitivity to another.
source: One possible strategy takes advantage of collateral sensitivity, in which resistance to one drug causes increased sensitivity to another (Baym et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Baym et al., 2016.

claim: The phenomenon of collateral sensitivity has been observed across various antibiotic classes in bacteria, as well as anti-fungals, and even cancer therapies.
source: The phenomenon of collateral sensitivity, or 'negative cross-resistance', has been observed across various antibiotic classes in bacteria, as well as anti-fungals, and even cancer therapies (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Rosenkilde et al., 2019; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Rank et al., 1975; Leroux et al., 2000; Dhawan et al., 2017; Lorendeau et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: When resistance to one inhibitor leads to collateral sensitivity to another, the two inhibitors can be used in a sequential cycling strategy to maintain sensitive bacterial populations.
source: Laboratory studies evaluating the evolution of resistance to antibiotics have demonstrated that when resistance to one inhibitor leads to collateral sensitivity to another, the two inhibitors can be used in a sequential cycling strategy to maintain sensitive bacterial populations (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Kim et al., 2014), or simultaneously in combination to slow or suppress the evolution of resistance (Gonzales et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Imamovic and Sommer, 2013 and Kim et al., 2014.

claim: Two inhibitors exhibiting collateral sensitivity can be used simultaneously in combination to slow or suppress the evolution of resistance.
source: Laboratory studies evaluating the evolution of resistance to antibiotics have demonstrated that when resistance to one inhibitor leads to collateral sensitivity to another, the two inhibitors can be used in a sequential cycling strategy to maintain sensitive bacterial populations (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Kim et al., 2014), or simultaneously in combination to slow or suppress the evolution of resistance (Gonzales et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014; Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gonzales et al., 2015; Munck et al., 2014; and Rodriguez de Evgrafov et al., 2015.

claim: Isoforms of the chloroquine resistance transporter (PfCRT) that transport chloroquine out of the parasite's digestive vacuole can cause increased sensitivity to a variety of compounds.
source: For example, isoforms of the chloroquine resistance transporter (PfCRT) that transport chloroquine out of the parasite's digestive vacuole can cause increased sensitivity to a variety of compounds (Lukens et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2004; Sisowath et al., 2009; Richards et al., 2016; Cooper et al., 2002; Evans and Havlik, 1993; Small-Saunders et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Collateral sensitivity has been observed between compounds targeting different subunits of the Plasmodium proteasome Pf20S.
source: Collateral sensitivity has also been observed between compounds targeting different subunits of the Plasmodium proteasome Pf20S (Kirkman et al., 2018; Stokes et al., 2019), between different chemotypes targeting the P-Type Cation-Transporter ATPase 4 (PfATP4) (Flannery et al., 2015), and between compounds targeting the Qo and Qi sites of cytochrome b (Lukens et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kirkman et al., 2018 and Stokes et al., 2019.

claim: Collateral sensitivity has been observed between different chemotypes targeting the P-Type Cation-Transporter ATPase 4 (PfATP4).
source: Collateral sensitivity has also been observed between compounds targeting different subunits of the Plasmodium proteasome Pf20S (Kirkman et al., 2018; Stokes et al., 2019), between different chemotypes targeting the P-Type Cation-Transporter ATPase 4 (PfATP4) (Flannery et al., 2015), and between compounds targeting the Qo and Qi sites of cytochrome b (Lukens et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Flannery et al., 2015.

claim: Collateral sensitivity has been observed between compounds targeting the Qo and Qi sites of cytochrome b.
source: Collateral sensitivity has also been observed between compounds targeting different subunits of the Plasmodium proteasome Pf20S (Kirkman et al., 2018; Stokes et al., 2019), between different chemotypes targeting the P-Type Cation-Transporter ATPase 4 (PfATP4) (Flannery et al., 2015), and between compounds targeting the Qo and Qi sites of cytochrome b (Lukens et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lukens et al., 2015.

claim: Collateral sensitivity occurs during the evolution of resistance to Plasmodium DHODH inhibitors, where mutations in dhodh conferring resistance to one inhibitor can alter the enzyme such that it becomes more sensitive to inhibition by other, structurally distinct compounds.
source: We have also previously shown that collateral sensitivity occurs during the evolution of resistance to Plasmodium DHODH inhibitors. Mutations in dhodh conferring resistance to one inhibitor can alter the enzyme such that it becomes more sensitive to inhibition by other, structurally distinct compounds (Lukens et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lukens et al., 2014 and Ross et al., 2014.

claim: Several compounds with increased activities against DHODH mutants relative to wildtype parasites were successfully identified from antimalarial libraries from GSK.
source: In an effort to expand this work, we screened antimalarial libraries from GSK, and successfully identified several compounds with increased activities against DHODH mutants relative to wildtype parasites (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Ross et al., 2018.

claim: TCMDC-125334 exhibited increased activity against all mutant lines tested, including those that arose during selection with DSM265.
source: We focused on the compound TCMDC-125334, a DHODH inhibitor that exhibited increased activity against all mutant lines tested, including those that arose during selection with the clinical candidate DSM265.
evidence: This is based on experimental dose-response data presented in the study.

claim: The DHODH C276Y, F227I, F227I/L527I, F227L, and F227L/L31F mutant lines have similar dose-response phenotypes.
source: Hierarchical clustering of this data reveals broad patterns of cross-resistance and collateral sensitivity. The DHODH C276Y, F227I, F227I/L527I, F227L, and F227L/L31F mutant lines have similar dose-response phenotypes.
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis of dose-response data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The DHODH E182D and I263F mutant lines share similar cross-resistance profiles.
source: The DHODH E182D and I263F mutant lines also share similar cross-resistance profiles, as we previously reported (Ross et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on cross-resistance analysis data and supported by a citation to Ross et al., 2018.

claim: The DHODH L531F mutant line has a unique sensitivity phenotype.
source: In contrast, the DHODH L531F mutant line has a unique sensitivity phenotype (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Five related triazolopyrimidine-based compounds (DSM265, DSM267, TCMDC-124402, TCMDC-124417, TCMDC-123826) cluster together, as all mutant lines show cross-resistance against these molecules.
source: This analysis also suggests some structure-activity relationships. Five related triazolopyrimidine-based compounds (DSM265, DSM267, TCMDC-124402, TCMDC-124417, TCMDC-123826) cluster together, as all mutant lines show cross-resistance against these molecules (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis and dose-response data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TCMDC-123823, TCMDC-123545, and TCMDC-123566 cluster together based on their activity profile and have a similar chemical structure.
source: TCMDC-123823, TCMDC-123545, and TCMDC-123566 also cluster together based on their activity profile, and have a similar chemical structure (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on hierarchical clustering analysis and chemical structure comparison.

claim: The eight mutant lines had varying degrees of sensitivity to TCMDC-125334, from DHODH I263F which is 1.3-fold more sensitive than the wildtype parent, to DHODH C276Y, which is 12-fold sensitive.
source: The eight mutant lines had varying degrees of sensitivity to this compound, from DHODH I263F which is 1.3-fold more sensitive than the wildtype parent, to DHODH C276Y, which is 12-fold sensitive.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data presented in the study.

claim: All mutant lines were at least 10-fold resistant to DSM265.
source: In contrast, all mutant lines were at least 10-fold resistant to DSM265 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Expression of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae cytosolic type I DHODH (ScDHODH) bypasses the mitochondrial DHODH enzyme, rendering blood-stage parasites insensitive to inhibitors that target electron transport chain proteins DHODH and cytochrome bc1.
source: Expression of the Saccharomyces cerevisiae cytosolic type I DHODH (ScDHODH) bypasses the mitochondrial DHODH enzyme, rendering blood-stage parasites insensitive to inhibitors that target electron transport chain proteins DHODH and cytochrome bc1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ScDHODH system used in target validation.

claim: Addition of proguanil has a potentiating effect for compounds that target cytochrome bc1, but not DHODH.
source: However, addition of proguanil has a potentiating effect for compounds that target cytochrome bc1, but not DHODH (Painter et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Painter et al., 2007.

claim: Expression of ScDHODH ablates the activity of TCMDC-125334.
source: We previously confirmed that expression of ScDHODH ablates the activity of TCMDC-125334, and that treating the ScDHODH line with TCMDC-125334 and proguanil in combination does not impact this activity (Ross et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ross et al., 2018 and Dong et al., 2011.

claim: Treating the ScDHODH line with TCMDC-125334 and proguanil in combination does not impact the activity of TCMDC-125334.
source: We previously confirmed that expression of ScDHODH ablates the activity of TCMDC-125334, and that treating the ScDHODH line with TCMDC-125334 and proguanil in combination does not impact this activity (Ross et al., 2018; Dong et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Ross et al., 2018 and Dong et al., 2011.

claim: After two rounds of treatment with TCMDC-125334, populations displayed moderate (~2-fold) resistance to TCMDC-125334.
source: After two rounds of treatment, populations displayed moderate (~2-fold) resistance to TCMDC-125334 (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Clonal lines isolated from flask 1 had two- or threefold copy number variation (CNV) encompassing the dhodh locus.
source: Clonal lines isolated from flask 1 had two- or threefold copy number variation (CNV) encompassing the dhodh locus, which corresponded to a two- or three-fold resistance phenotype to TCMDC-125334, as well as to the structurally distinct DHODH inhibitors DSM265, Genz669178, and IDI6273.
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing and qPCR data presented in the study.

claim: Two- or threefold copy number variation of dhodh corresponded to a two- or three-fold resistance phenotype to TCMDC-125334, as well as to the structurally distinct DHODH inhibitors DSM265, Genz669178, and IDI6273.
source: Clonal lines isolated from flask 1 had two- or threefold copy number variation (CNV) encompassing the dhodh locus, which corresponded to a two- or three-fold resistance phenotype to TCMDC-125334, as well as to the structurally distinct DHODH inhibitors DSM265, Genz669178, and IDI6273.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data and genetic analysis presented in the study.

claim: Four clones isolated from flask 2 did not have a resistance phenotype and had no genetic changes in the dhodh locus.
source: Of the clones isolated from flask 2, four did not have a resistance phenotype, and had no genetic changes in the dhodh locus (Figure 2C–F, Table 1, Supplementary file 1b, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Table 1—source data 1, Table 1—source data 2, Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assays and whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: Clone T-F2-C1 was 3-fold resistant to TCMDC-125334 and Genz669178, and 13-fold resistant to IDI-6273.
source: One clone, T-F2-C1, was 3-fold resistant to TCMDC-125334 and Genz669178, and 13-fold resistant to IDI-6273 (Figure 2C–F, Table 1, Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Clone T-F2-C1 had a point mutation resulting in a DHODH I263S amino acid change.
source: Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) revealed that clone T-F2-C1 had a point mutation resulting in a DHODH I263S amino acid change (Table 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing data.

claim: The DHODH I263S parasite line remained sensitive to DSM265.
source: Notably, this DHODH I263S parasite line remained sensitive to DSM265 (Figure 2D, Table 1, Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1.

claim: Parasite populations exhibited 2x copy number variation of the dhodh locus after the first round of treatment with TCMDC-125334.
source: Genetic characterization revealed that parasite populations exhibited 2x copy number variation of the dhodh locus after the first round of treatment with TCMDC-125334, and five- to eight-fold copy number variation of the dhodh locus after the second round of treatment (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on qPCR and whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Parasite populations exhibited five- to eight-fold copy number variation of the dhodh locus after the second round of treatment with TCMDC-125334.
source: Genetic characterization revealed that parasite populations exhibited 2x copy number variation of the dhodh locus after the first round of treatment with TCMDC-125334, and five- to eight-fold copy number variation of the dhodh locus after the second round of treatment (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on qPCR and whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Parasites resistant to DSM265 emerged rapidly after just one round of treatment, after 7 days in compound-free media.
source: As previously observed, parasites resistant to DSM265 emerged rapidly after just one round of treatment, after 7 days in compound-free media (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from the current study and supported by a citation to Mandt et al., 2019.

claim: The minimum inoculation of resistance for DSM265 is 10^5.5.
source: This was expected given that the minimum inoculation of resistance for DSM265 is 105.5 (Duffey et al., 2021), and we use 108 parasites in our selection experiments.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Duffey et al., 2021.

claim: Whole-genome sequencing of bulk populations selected with DSM265 revealed two point mutations in dhodh—DHODH C276Y and I273M.
source: WGS of the bulk populations revealed two point mutations in dhodh—DHODH C276Y and I273M (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1c, Figure 2—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Selections with two distinct DHODH inhibitors, Genz666136 and DSM74, yielded resistant parasites with a DHODH E182D mutation, which were hypersensitive to the DHODH inhibitor IDI-6273.
source: In our previous work, selections with two distinct DHODH inhibitors, Genz666136 and DSM74, yielded resistant parasites with a DHODH E182D mutation, which were hypersensitive to the DHODH inhibitor IDI-6273.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental data from the authors' prior work.

claim: When DHODH E182D parasites were treated with IDI-6273, parasites reverted to the wildtype D182 protein sequence, albeit with a different DNA codon.
source: When we treated the DHODH E182D parasite line with IDI-6273, parasites reverted to the wildtype D182 protein sequence, albeit with a different DNA codon.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental data from the authors' prior work.

claim: The D182E revertant line had a sensitivity phenotype similar to wildtype parasites.
source: The D182E revertant line had a sensitivity phenotype similar to wildtype parasites (Lukens et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Lukens et al., 2014.

claim: Resistance was observed in all three bulk parasite populations recovered from the second pulse of TCMDC-125334 treatment of DHODH C276Y parasites.
source: Resistance was observed in all three bulk parasite populations recovered from this second pulse (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Sequentially selected parasites were less sensitive to TCMDC-125334 relative to the DHODH C276Y parental line, but were still more sensitive than Pf3D7 A10 parasites with a wildtype dhodh sequence.
source: While these parasites were less sensitive to TCMDC-125334 relative to the DHODH C276Y parental line, they were still more sensitive than Pf3D7 A10 parasites with a wildtype dhodh sequence (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Clones isolated from sequentially selected populations had an intermediate dose-response phenotype for TCMDC-125334.
source: Clones isolated from these sequentially selected populations had a similar intermediate dose-response phenotype for TCMDC-125334 (Figure 3D and E, Table 2, Supplementary file 1d, Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 3D and Table 2.

claim: Compared to the DHODH C276Y parent, sequentially selected clones had greatly increased resistance to DSM265, with EC50's>200 nM.
source: However, compared to the DHODH C276Y parent, they had greatly increased resistance to DSM265, with EC50's>200 nM (Figure 3E, Table 2, Supplementary file 1d, Table 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 3E and Table 2.

claim: Parasites sequentially selected with TCMDC-125334 retained the DHODH C276Y mutation and gained additional mutations in dhodh, rather than reverting back to wildtype.
source: WGS revealed that parasites retained the DHODH C276Y mutation, and gained additional mutations in dhodh, rather than reverting back to wildtype (Table 2, Table 2—source data 2, Table 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2.

claim: Clones isolated from flask 1 and flask 2 of the sequential selection had increased dhodh copy number, in addition to the DHODH C276Y mutation.
source: Clones isolated from flask 1 and flask 2 had increased dhodh copy number, in addition to the DHODH C276Y mutation, as confirmed by qPCR (Table 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on qPCR and whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Table 2.

claim: Clones from flask 3 of the sequential selection had gained an additional F227Y mutation.
source: Clones from flask 3 had gained an additional F227Y mutation (Table 2, Table 2—source data 3).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2.

claim: Sequential selection of a DSM265-resistant line with TCMDC-125334 does not restore sensitivity to DSM265.
source: Overall, sequential selection of a DSM265-resistant line with TCMDC-125334 does not restore sensitivity to DSM265.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dose-response data from the sequential selection experiments.

claim: Sequentially selected parasites with additional mutations in dhodh were highly resistant to DSM265 but were not cross-resistant to TCMDC-125334.
source: While sequentially selected parasites with additional mutations in dhodh were highly resistant to DSM265, they were not cross-resistant to TCMDC-125334, suggesting that they would still be sensitive to a therapeutic dose.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data from the sequential selection experiments.

claim: The DHODH C276Y mutation alone is ~10-fold resistant to DMS265 and ~10-fold sensitive to TCMDC-125334 compared to wildtype.
source: Compared to wildtype, the DHODH C276Y mutation alone is ~10-fold resistant to DMS265, and ~10-fold sensitive to TCMDC-125334 (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Table 3.

claim: The DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant is ~1000-fold resistant to DSM265.
source: In contrast, the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant is ~1000-fold resistant to DSM265.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Table 3.

claim: The DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant line is still ~2-fold sensitive to TCMDC-125334 relative to wildtype.
source: However, the double mutant line is still ~2-fold sensitive to TCMDC-125334 relative to wildtype.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Table 3.

claim: The DHODH F227Y mutant line exhibited three-fold resistance to TCMDC-125334.
source: We characterized the dose-response phenotype of the DHODH F227Y mutant line and found that it exhibited three-fold resistance to TCMDC-125334 (Table 3, Table 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Table 3.

claim: The phenotype of the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant is consistent with additivity, ruling out a negative epistatic interaction.
source: Comparing the dose-response phenotype of the single mutant lines DHODH C276Y and DHODH F227Y to the phenotype of the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant, we find that the phenotype of the two mutations in combination is consistent with additivity, ruling out a negative epistatic interaction (Figure 3F–I, Table 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of dose-response data comparing single and double mutants shown in Figure 3F-I and Table 3.

claim: After three pulses of compound treatment totaling 63–73 days with DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 combination, two populations cross-resistant to both compounds were obtained.
source: However, after three pulses of compound treatment totaling 63–73 days, we obtained two populations cross-resistant to both compounds (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from combination selection experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Three of the four clonal lines isolated from flask 1 of the combination selection were moderately (~2-fold) resistant to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334, as well as Genz669178 and IDI-6273.
source: Three of the four clonal lines isolated from flask 1 were moderately (~2-fold) resistant to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334, as well as Genz669178 and IDI-6273 (Figure 4D–G, Table 4, Supplementary file 1e, Table 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 4D-G and Table 4.

claim: Copy number duplication of the dhodh locus was detected in resistant clones from flask 1 by qPCR and WGS.
source: Copy number duplication of the dhodh locus was detected in these resistant clones by qPCR and WGS (Table 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Table 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is based on qPCR and whole-genome sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Table 4.

claim: All six clones isolated from flask 2 of the combination selection were four- to sixfold resistant to TCMDC-125334 and 16- to 20-fold resistant to DSM265.
source: All six clones isolated from flask 2 were four- to sixfold resistant to TCMDC-125334 and 16- to 20-fold resistant to DSM265.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 4D-E and Table 4.

claim: Clones from flask 2 of the combination selection were ~2-fold resistant to IDI-6273, but were still sensitive to Genz669178.
source: These clones were also ~2-fold resistant to IDI-6273, but were still sensitive to Genz669178 (Figure 4D–G, Table 4, Supplementary file 1e, Table 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data shown in Figure 4F-G and Table 4.

claim: All six clones from flask 2 of the combination selection had the same point mutation resulting in a DHODH V532A amino acid change.
source: Sequencing revealed that these six clones had the same point mutation resulting in a DHODH V532A amino acid change (Table 4—source data 3, Table 4—source data 4).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing and Sanger sequencing data shown in Table 4.

claim: Resistance took longer to emerge with combination treatment compared to treatment with DSM265 or TCMC-125334 alone (63–73 days with combination treatment vs. 43 days with TCMDC-125334 alone and 16 days with DSM265 alone).
source: Thus, although resistance took longer to emerge with combination treatment compared to treatment with DSM265 or TCMC-125334 alone (63–73 days with combination treatment vs. 43 days with TCMDC-125334 alone and 16 days with DSM265 alone), this strategy was ultimately insufficient to prevent the emergence of parasites resistant to both compounds.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data from different selection experiments.

claim: Combination treatment with DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 was ultimately insufficient to prevent the emergence of parasites resistant to both compounds.
source: Thus, although resistance took longer to emerge with combination treatment compared to treatment with DSM265 or TCMC-125334 alone (63–73 days with combination treatment vs. 43 days with TCMDC-125334 alone and 16 days with DSM265 alone), this strategy was ultimately insufficient to prevent the emergence of parasites resistant to both compounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from combination selection experiments.

claim: The best pose predicted by molecular docking simulations shows that TCMDC-125334 docks within same hydrophobic binding pocket as DSM265 and other DHODH inhibitors.
source: The best pose predicted by our simulations shows that TCMDC-125334 docks within same hydrophobic binding pocket as DSM265 and other DHODH inhibitors (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is based on in silico molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 5.

claim: TCMDC-125334 binds allosterically with regard to both orotate/dihydroorotate and FMN.
source: As with all published crystal structures of DHODH inhibitors, our simulations suggest that TCMDC-125334 binds allosterically with regard to both orotate/dihydroorotate and FMN.
evidence: This is based on in silico molecular docking simulations and comparison with published crystal structures.

claim: Molecular docking results suggest that the DHODHV532A mutation would disrupt hydrophobic interactions with the furan and 1,3,4-oxadiazole rings.
source: Our docking results suggest that the DHODHV532A mutation would disrupt hydrophobic interactions with the furan and 1,3,4-oxadiazole rings, consistent with the observed 5.3-fold resistance seen with the DHODHV532A mutants.
evidence: This is based on in silico molecular docking simulations and is consistent with experimental dose-response data.

claim: Molecular simulation predicted that the DHODHC276Y mutant would have higher affinity for TCMDC-125334 than wildtype.
source: Our simulation predicted that the DHODHC276Y mutant would have higher affinity for TCMDC-125334 than wildtype.
evidence: This is based on in silico molecular docking simulations.

claim: The DHODH V532A variant remained at ~50% frequency over time in competitive growth assays.
source: This analysis showed that the DHODH V532A variant remained at ~50% frequency over time (Figure 6, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome sequencing data from competitive growth assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: On day 0, the mixed culture of DHODH V532A and wildtype exhibited an intermediate dose-response phenotype, as illustrated by a biphasic dose-response curve, and this intermediate phenotype was maintained at day 28.
source: On day 0, the mixed culture exhibited an intermediate dose-response phenotype, as illustrated by a biphasic dose-response curve. This intermediate phenotype was maintained at day 28 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data from competitive growth assays shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the genotypic and phenotypic data indicate that the DHODH V532A mutant is as fit as wildtype parasites.
source: Overall, both the genotypic and phenotypic data indicate that the DHODH V532A mutant is as fit as wildtype parasites.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on competitive growth assay data (genotypic and phenotypic).

claim: Combining two DHODH inhibitors, DSM265 and TCDC-125334, based on their collateral sensitivity profiles fails to prevent the emergence of resistance in P. falciparum in vitro.
source: The main conclusion of our study is that combining two DHODH inhibitors, DSM265 and TCDC-125334, based on their collateral sensitivity profiles fails to prevent the emergence of resistance in P. falciparum in vitro.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on experimental data from combination selection experiments.

claim: The DHODH F227Y mutation alone confers resistance to TCMDC-125334.
source: We found that sequentially treating a collaterally sensitive mutant line with TCMDC-125334 selected for parasites with additional genetic changes in dhodh, including the DHODH F227Y mutation, which alone also confers resistance to TCMDC-125334.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data from the sequential selection experiments.

claim: The DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant is less sensitive than the DHODH C276Y parent, but is still more sensitive to TCMDC-125334 compared to wildtype parasites.
source: While the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant is less sensitive than the DHODH C276Y parent, it is still more sensitive to TCMDC-125334 compared to wildtype parasites.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data comparing the double mutant to the single mutant and wildtype.

claim: The DHODH V532A mutation does not exhibit a fitness cost in in vitro competitive growth assays.
source: We also demonstrated that the DHODH V532A mutation does not exhibit a fitness cost in in vitro competitive growth assays.
evidence: This is based on competitive growth assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: CNV was a common mechanism of resistance to TCMDC-125334 across multiple independent selections.
source: While we identified three point mutations in this study that confer resistance to TCMDC-125334, the majority of dhodh mutations tested thus far are sensitive to this molecule. CNV was a common mechanism of resistance to TCMDC-125334 across multiple independent selections.
evidence: This is based on genetic analysis data from multiple selection experiments.

claim: Three of four populations of wildtype 3D7 A10 selected with TCMDC-125334 exhibited increased copy number of dhodh.
source: Three of four populations of wildtype 3D7 A10 selected with TCMDC-125334 exhibited increased copy number of dhodh.
evidence: This is based on qPCR and whole-genome sequencing data from selection experiments.

claim: When the collaterally sensitive DHODH C276Y line was selected with TCMDC-125334, clones isolated from two of three independent populations exhibited two- to fourfold CNV of dhodh.
source: When we selected the collaterally sensitive DHODH C276Y line with TCMDC-125334, clones isolated from two of three independent populations exhibited two- to fourfold CNV of dhodh.
evidence: This is based on qPCR and whole-genome sequencing data from sequential selection experiments.

claim: The majority of in vitro selections with DSM265 and DSM267 selected for point mutations in the dhodh locus, with CNVs occurring only seldomly.
source: In contrast to this, the majority of in vitro selections with DSM265 and DSM267 selected for point mutations in the dhodh locus, with CNVs occurring only seldomly (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandt et al., 2019.

claim: CNVs confer cross-resistance across various DHODH inhibitor compound classes, but this mechanism confers only moderately reduced susceptibility.
source: While CNVs confers cross-resistance across various DHODH inhibitor compound classes, this mechanism confers only moderately reduced susceptibility.
evidence: This is based on dose-response data from parasites with CNV at the dhodh locus.

claim: CNVs are less evolutionarily stable compared to point mutations.
source: CNVs are also less evolutionarily stable compared to point mutations.
evidence: This is general knowledge about the stability of different types of genetic changes.

claim: Additional copies of dhodh are lost in in vitro culture over time.
source: Others have shown that additional copies of dhodh are lost in in vitro culture over time (Guler et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guler et al., 2013.

claim: Selecting DHODH E182D parasites with the mutant-type inhibitor IDI-6273 caused parasites to revert back to the wildtype amino acid sequence.
source: This result is in contrast with our previous work, in which selecting DHODH E182D parasites with the mutant-type inhibitor IDI-6273 caused parasites to revert back to the wildtype amino acid sequence.
evidence: This is based on previous experimental data from the authors' prior work.

claim: The DHODH E182D parasite had a competitive fitness defect.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that the DHODH E182D parasite had a competitive fitness defect (Lukens et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2014), while we previously showed that the DHODH C276Y is as fit as wildtype in in vitro competitive growth assays (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lukens et al., 2014 and Ross et al., 2014.

claim: The DHODH C276Y is as fit as wildtype in in vitro competitive growth assays.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that the DHODH E182D parasite had a competitive fitness defect (Lukens et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2014), while we previously showed that the DHODH C276Y is as fit as wildtype in in vitro competitive growth assays (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandt et al., 2019.

claim: Differing evolutionary outcomes (reversion vs. secondary mutation) may be due to differences in the fitness cost of the initial resistance mutations.
source: Previous research on collateral sensitivity in Pseudomonas aeruginosa from Barbosa et al. suggests that differing evolutionary outcomes (reversion vs. secondary mutation) may be due to differences in the fitness cost of the initial resistance mutations (Barbosa et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Barbosa et al., 2019.

claim: The competitively fit DHODH C276Y line favored alternative pathways to cross-resistance rather than reversion to wildtype.
source: Similarly, we saw that the competitively fit DHODH C276Y line favored alternative pathways to cross-resistance rather than reversion to wildtype.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from sequential selection experiments.

claim: Treatment with a second compound can result in the acquisition of additional genetic changes and subsequent multidrug resistance.
source: However, our results suggest that treatment with a second compound can also result in the acquisition of additional genetic changes and subsequent multidrug resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from sequential selection experiments.

claim: The two mutations in the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant exhibit additive epistasis.
source: Comparing the phenotype of the DHDOH C276Y/F227Y double mutant with DHODH C276Y and DHODH F227Y parasite lines, we also note that the two mutations in combination exhibit additive epistasis.
evidence: This is based on analysis of dose-response data comparing single and double mutants.

claim: Additive epistasis resulted in markedly high-level resistance to DSM265 (>1000-fold relative to wildtype) in the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant.
source: This resulted in markedly high-level resistance to DSM265 (>1000-fold relative to wildtype).
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data for the double mutant.

claim: Epistasis is an important factor in determining the evolution of resistance and cross-resistance/collateral sensitivity.
source: Multiple studies indicate that epistasis is an important factor in determining the evolution of resistance and cross-resistance/collateral sensitivity (Rosenkilde et al., 2019; Barbosa et al., 2019; Apjok et al., 2019; Lozovsky et al., 2009; Dellus-Gur et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Negative epistasis between resistance mutations within the same enzyme constrains the number of pathways to higher-level resistance.
source: Negative epistasis between resistance mutations within the same enzyme constrains the number of pathways to higher-level resistance (Lozovsky et al., 2009; Dellus-Gur et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lozovsky et al., 2009 and Dellus-Gur et al., 2015.

claim: Re-sensitization to wildtype is favored when there is negative epistasis between resistance mechanisms.
source: In the context of collateral sensitivity, the study from Barbosa et al., 2019 also indicates that re-sensitization to wildtype is favored when there is negative epistasis between resistance mechanisms.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Barbosa et al., 2019.

claim: Under additive epistasis, the emergence of an initial resistance mutation can open up pathways to higher-level resistance.
source: In contrast, our result highlights how, under additive epistasis, the emergence of an initial resistance mutation can open up pathways to higher-level resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed additive epistasis in the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant.

claim: Combination treatment with DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 failed to suppress resistance due to the great diversity of evolutionarily competitive dhodh mutations that confer resistance to various inhibitors.
source: The major take-away of this study is that combination treatment with DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 failed to suppress resistance, and we hypothesize that this is due to the great diversity of evolutionarily competitive dhodh mutations that confer resistance to various inhibitors.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental results and analysis of the diversity of resistance mutations.

claim: Observed patterns of collateral sensitivity are often thwarted due to the existence of diverse trajectories to resistance.
source: Other reports in bacteria have also found that observed patterns of collateral sensitivity are often thwarted due to the existence of diverse trajectories to resistance.
evidence: This is general knowledge from the literature on collateral sensitivity in bacteria.

claim: When selections are repeated enough times or are performed with a large enough starting populations, cross-resistant variants eventually emerge, even if they are relatively rare.
source: When selections are repeated enough times (Nichol et al., 2019), or are performed with a large enough starting populations (Jiao et al., 2016), cross-resistant variants eventually emerge, even if they are relatively rare.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Nichol et al., 2019 and Jiao et al., 2016.

claim: Although most of the mutations originally identified were collaterally sensitive to TCMDC-125334, repeated treatment with DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 in combination ultimately yielded the cross-resistant variant DHODH V532A.
source: Similarly, we find that although most of the mutations we originally identified were collaterally sensitive to TCMDC-125334, repeated treatment with DSM265 and TCMDC-125334 in combination ultimately yielded the cross-resistant variant DHODH V532A.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from combination selection experiments.

claim: The DHODH V532A mutation conferring cross-resistance to both compounds emerged from a population of 10^8 parasites after three treatment cycles.
source: However, we did find that the DHODH V532A mutation conferring cross-resistance to both compounds emerged from a population of 108 parasites after three treatment cycles.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from combination selection experiments.

claim: There can be 10^10–10^13 parasites in an infected human host.
source: In contrast, there can be 1010–1013 parasites in an infected human host, suggesting that this would be a sufficient population size for cross-resistance to emerge (Goldberg et al., 2012; Bopp et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Goldberg et al., 2012 and Bopp et al., 2013.

claim: A population of 10^10–10^13 parasites in an infected human host would be a sufficient population size for cross-resistance to emerge.
source: In contrast, there can be 1010–1013 parasites in an infected human host, suggesting that this would be a sufficient population size for cross-resistance to emerge (Goldberg et al., 2012; Bopp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of the population size used in the study (10^8) where cross-resistance emerged, and the larger population size in an infected human.

claim: Prior to this work, 13 individual point mutations and 2 sets of double mutations that conferred resistance to DHODH had been identified.
source: This study also highlights the flexibility of the DHODH enzyme. Prior to this work, we had identified 13 individual point mutations and 2 sets of double mutations that conferred resistance to DHODH.
evidence: This is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: In this study, two additional point mutations—DHODH I263S and DHODH V532A—as well as the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant line were selected.
source: In this study, we selected two additional point mutations—DHODH I263S and DHODH V532A—as well as the DHODH C276Y/F227Y double mutant line.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from resistance selection experiments in the study.

claim: The DHODH I263S mutation is not resistant to DSM265, while the DHODH I263F mutation at the same site confers strong (~100-fold) resistance to this compound.
source: Interestingly, the DHODH I263S mutation is not resistant to DSM265, while the DHODH I263F mutation at the same site confers strong (~100-fold) resistance to this compound.
evidence: This is based on dose-response assay data comparing the two mutations.

claim: Previous studies have crystallized the DHODH enzyme bound to various inhibitors, including DMS265 (PDB 4RX0), Genz669178 (PDB 4CQ8), and IDI-6273 (PDB 4CQA).
source: Previous studies have crystallized the DHODH enzyme bound to various inhibitors, including DMS265 (PDB 4RX0), Genz669178 (PDB 4CQ8), and IDI-6273 (PDB 4CQA) (Phillips et al., 2015; Lukens et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Phillips et al., 2015 and Lukens et al., 2014.

claim: DSM265, Genz669178, and IDI-6273 all bind within the same flexible pocket of the DHODH enzyme.
source: These compounds all bind within the same flexible pocket (see Figure 1A) of the enzyme.
evidence: This is based on crystal structure data shown in Figure 1A and cited literature.

claim: The inhibitor binding pocket of DHODH accommodates the binding of a variety of chemical structures and is very mutationally flexible.
source: Our results demonstrate that this pocket not only accommodates the binding of a variety of chemical structures, but is also very mutationally flexible, highlighting the resistance liability of this enzyme as a drug target.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diversity of inhibitors that bind to the pocket and the diversity of resistance mutations identified.

claim: Molecular simulation studies provided insight into the potential mechanism of resistance to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334, highlighting the interactions at position V532.
source: Molecular simulation studies provided insight into the potential mechanism of resistance to both DSM265 and TCMDC-125334, highlighting the interactions at position V532.
evidence: This is based on in silico molecular docking simulations.

claim: Understanding the mechanism of collateral sensitivity will require further study.
source: However, understanding the mechanism of collateral sensitivity will require further study.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study and the need for future work.

claim: Molecular simulation points to differential binding affinity of TCMDC-125334 to the wildtype and C276Y mutant proteins, consistent with the increased sensitivity of the mutant observed in the study.
source: Molecular simulation points to differential binding affinity of TCMDC-125334 to the wildtype and C276Y mutant proteins, consistent with the increased sensitivity of the mutant observed in our study (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on in silico molecular docking simulations shown in Figure 5 and is consistent with experimental dose-response data.

claim: With DSM265 alone, the in vitro data is a good predictor of the in vivo evolution of resistance.
source: We previously demonstrated that with DSM265 alone, the in vitro data is a good predictor of the in vivo evolution of resistance (Mandt et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Mandt et al., 2019.

claim: It will be important to test potential combination strategies in vivo, as pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics may impact how multiple drugs interact with each other, with implications for the emergence of resistance.
source: It will be important to test potential combination strategies in vivo, as pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics may impact how multiple drugs interact with each other, with implications for the emergence of resistance.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for future in vivo studies.

claim: Additional mutational pathways to resistance could potentially be identified through further resistance selections or high-throughput methods such as deep mutational scanning to assess variants.
source: However, our continued identification of novel point mutations in the dhodh locus suggests that we still have not saturated the dhodh resistome. Additional mutational pathways to resistance could potentially be identified through further resistance selections or high-throughput methods such as deep mutational scanning to assess variants.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study and suggestions for future work.

claim: The mutational flexibility of the inhibitor binding site in DHODH increases the likelihood of resistance to any compound or compound combination that targets this site.
source: The mutational flexibility of the inhibitor binding site in DHODH increases the likelihood of resistance to any compound or compound combination that targets this site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the diversity of resistance mutations identified in the study.

claim: CNV appears to be a general mechanism of resistance to multiple chemical classes of DHODH inhibitors.
source: CNV also appears to be a general mechanism of resistance to multiple chemical classes of DHODH inhibitors.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing CNV as a resistance mechanism across different DHODH inhibitors.

claim: Targeting DHODH with antimalarial drugs has a high risk of resistance emergence.
source: One implication of these results is that targeting this enzyme with antimalarial drugs has a high risk of resistance emergence and brings into question the usefulness of pursuing further DHODH inhibitors.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results showing the diversity and ease of resistance emergence.
